text:
After playing this game on and off for over a decade (even though the playtime wouldn’t really suggest it), I have come to the conclusion that this game should be taken off life support, something Valve would obviously celebrate, as evidenced by complete disregard of the player base time and time again.

Team Fortress 2 is so, so painfully a product of its time, where “its time” is every single time Valve pushed out a large update. We got cosmetics (also limited-time ones, given for arbitrary reasons) and microtransactions, then matchmaking and some perverse version of achievements with rewards (Jungle Inferno contracts, anyone?) Finally, we settled on rampant cheating. If I could, I would instead write a review on Valve Anti-Cheat, but here we are…

Botting on TF2 got so bad that it was impossible to play, which is something that Valve doesn’t care about anymore if there’s profit in there somewhere. It was only after the community rallied together that Valve “fixed” the issue, but, to this day, if you play long enough and pay enough attention, you will run into more “subtle” cheaters every few games, because commercial solutions exist to cater to such audiences (see: LMAOBOX). Valve’s “anti-cheat” can be completely bypassed by existing open-source code snippets, leading us back to the point that TF2 is truly a product of its time, where basic detection techniques were good enough and everything else past that was duct-taped on top. Now, with the game being maintained by a skeleton crew, there is simply no hope of the situation ever improving. There might be further instances of grand ban waves, but, in the end, it's a war of attrition that Valve will lose.

Taking a small detour on to other things stemming from the game’s age - if you’ve played Quake about as long as TF2, you’ll be experiencing a familiar aura of “the meta must not be broken” throughout several game modes (“ye intel shalt not be capped” in CTF and “thou shalt not suck” in Mann Up), not to mention getting destroyed by players with thousands upon thousands of hours spent playing, who may or may not be cheating. Despite all that, there are always new players to be found. Bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, they try to have fun in whatever way they see fit, but the more grizzled veterans know that having newbies in your team means getting stomped in a match.

“Why?”, you ask, “doesn’t the matchmaking system use some sort of rating to balance things out? Aren’t teams rebalanced if someone leaves or joins?”

*sigh*

text:
Team Fortress 2 is one of my favorite games and hat simulators of all time. It's not really much of a secret, given how many hours I've gotten in it plus the fact I've been playing it for over 10 years (although it was a while before I had a computer that could run it very well). It is more than just a game; it is a whole experience.

The gameplay is very addictive. The gunplay and counters feel just right, and no two classes play the same (which can't be said for some modern hero shooters). Team Fortress 2 showed that you only needed 9 classes maximum, instead of 20 or so. There are crates and microtransactions sure, but they aren't exactly forced upon you; you can simply get free item drops by just playing the game on servers (at least if they are secure VAC-enabled ones). A lot of the maps are very memorable; 2Fort, Dustbowl, Badwater etc. and a dozen of community created maps that would be too much to list here. Even with (non-cheating) singleplayer bots, the game is still very fun.

Personality and style wise, TF2 had the best a shooter game could ever have. The classes are all fun to witness, and even 17 years later they still feel irreplaceable, with perfect voice acting and beyond memorable and hilarious dialog. It's not like some other games where they are just generic, too. Each class was designed with shapes and silhouettes in mind, creating easily identifiable looks (i.e. if someone is outlined behind a wall, you could tell which class it is even from afar). The art-style of the game, inspired by J.C. Leyendecker, really made it timeless, and it still looks good to this day; an incredible feat for a game from 2007, a time when most games went for a muddy realistic look (a large portion of which haven't aged well visually). TF2 went for a heavily researched mixture of being cartoony and grounded, and it worked very, VERY well. It's not like some modern cartoony shooters that don't have reason behind the style, because this one does. There is also a story that is not forced upon you, being told through item descriptions, map objects, comics and shorts. It is wacky and adds a lot more to the game's world.

Now sure, the game has had its rough times. The Meet Your Match update was an attempt at making TF2 appeal to the e-sports scene, when really it was a game that you could pick up and just... play (hence why Quickplay was a thing). There was (currently remedied) also the botting crisis that lead to all sorts of different things (drama, campaigns, review bombings etc.). None of these affect my opinion on the game itself, however. You don't HAVE to play on Casual and Competitive; you can make your own server or join community ones. I only have minor criticisms with some weapon balancing decisions and bugs, but they aren't enough to lower my thoughts on the game. I do also wish that the classes had more unique lines for interacting with each other, rather than them being stuck to domination lines (think Left 4 Dead 2 or even Overwatch, where characters would refer to each other by name and talk if nearby).

I feel this review was long, long overdue (10 years overdue, even). I never really made serious reviews until now, but I figured I'd finally do so. Team Fortress 2 is not only one of the most important shooters, but also one of the most important games alone to me. It's a game that will never die to me, because even if the official servers shut off, you can still host your own and get others to join or play with singleplayer bots. Even playing with stock weapons is still fun. I'll probably still be playing in a decade or more from now. It just never gets old, even 17 years later.

   Even with all that there's lots to enjoy here. A shooter where firefights are more than a milisecond, unique playstyles, gamemodes, and communites. I still probably consider this my favorite game, it's just gotten too disheartening playing in this state. Let me say this.
Team Fortress 2 is a good game.
I adore so many things about this game, to the point where it is one of my favourite games of all time, even if I'm still not good at it. The movement is rock solid, the characters and art style is amazing, the type of stuff you can do with the guns in the game is amazing and, at the time, unlike anything the world had ever seen at that point. It was, and still is, nothing like I've ever played.
..LazyPurple made the point a lot better.
But.
In it's current state, TF2 has been objectively left to rot in the sun on the Sahara Desert by Valve. As you've probably heard, the Casual Mode has been overrun by bots that pick one of the classes, most of the time Sniper, and have them spin in the air until an enemy appears, only then do they use the aimbot that is packaged with the bots (they pick Sniper because if you land a headshot, it can be a one hit kill to most classes, unless when the gun is charged by being scoped in, which is why they spin in a circle, then it becomes all classes). The bots also spam the chat with opportunities to advertise "services" protect being aimbotted (which is just forking over money and being scammed), as well as spamming the text and in-game voice chat with hateful messages, voices that were artificially created, and have them saying slurs.

This isn't like Half-Life 2 Episode 3 where they don't announce anything for, at this point, over 17 years. And even THAT doesn't work as the bots purchase something AND THEN spam Casual lobbies.
None of this is coming from a place of hatred either. Granted, I haven't even played any Valve game from start to finish until 2021. But instead we don't know what's going on right now. megascatterbomb's findings proves that if Valve tried, they can fix this, relatively quickly. But no. Why bother?

text:
[i][b]UPDATE[/b] 7/10/2024:[/i] There have been a number of accounts asserting that the majority of the bots in this game have been banned, and official servers are largely clean now. This is great. It's delightful to see the pathetic bot hosters receive the hammer, squirming in their chairs and [i]hopefully[/i] questioning their life choices. Nonetheless, if you still care about this game, don't say "thanks", only say "good job". As long as the official game and inventory servers continue to run, they require maintenance, and I affirm this obvious fact with personal experience running my own web and mail servers. Do not buy from Mann Co. or any of Valve's other in-game microtransaction stores, primarily because it is important to keep the pressure on (and they are a large reason why the game was so botted to begin with). Persist, and surely you will see to it that one day you get your game back.

Team Fortress 2 was a favorite pasttime for an entire generation getting home from school every weekday. Unlike the more competitive multiplayer games, it never demanded too much from the player like it was some lifelong commitment to tie one's self up in. Even if you had never played this game back then, you may have seen the iconic nine classes appear in countless Garry's Mod and SFM skits over the years. The fact that the characters here have achieved such a level of ubiquity without the need for billion dollar marketing is a display of how brilliant the art direction was.

Certainly, this was one of the first games which convinced me of the merits of the first person shooter, and one of the first which got me into Steam to begin with. I've poured several hundred hours in here screwing around in various servers and generally having a good time. That was up until 2016... in my specific case, it had more to do with my interests shifting, but I did touch it exactly once more in 2018, well after that notorious failure of an update which tried to pull TF2 away from its roots and into more of a competitive game on the level of Counter-Strike and Dota. I wasn't pleased with how it seemed to become sterilized in such a manner. So, I turned away, uninstalled the game, cashed out my measly inventory a few years later, and never looked back, not feeling much from it...

So then, why now am I writing about this game? If you're not already aware, the official servers for Team Fortress 2 have been neglected to such an egregious extent for the past five years that even I cannot simply tune it out, having formerly been a rigorous player. These servers are heavily infested with bots which are intently designed to render the game unplayable. They're aimbotting, impersonating real users, spamming vile rhetoric, kicking players out, and largely eluding Valve's anti-cheat system all the way through. That's only scratching the surface; if you look it up yourself, you'll see it gets a whole lot worse.

What has Valve done about this? Nothing much, really. Actually, in recent times since the #SaveTF2 movement, they've done worse than nothing. Not only have they made no recent effort whatsoever to combat the bots, they now have the nerve to introduce new microtransaction products to TF2's store as they neglect the game. So, it's gone from apathy or laziness to pure spite.

Yes, I know. You can play in the community servers, which are much more proactive in keeping the bots out, often using freely available modules to aid in the process. But for the average person who doesn't look too much into things, they won't think this is a thing. The official servers effectively represent the game, and if they're unusable, so is the entire game for them.

For a multi-billion dollar corporation, this is pathetic. I had a lot of faith in Valve before, because they held onto some form of a "don't be evil" philosophy for a long time. I've made tons of excuses to myself that there was some good cause to some of their more questionable practices, like maybe the so-called "Mann-Conomy" was a tip jar so that one day we'd get an incredible new game from them. Oh, dear...

Recent leaks suggest Valve is planning to release a new game which is apparently a confusing salad of already established ideas from completely different games. It looks generic, but that's not what I intend to highlight here. With TF2 becoming a completely unsafe environment, and even Counter-Strike 2 suffering similar neglect, how can anyone be expected to have confidence in such a new game? At the rate things are going, it's bound to be dead on arrival.

You can invalidate me all you want with how I haven't touched the game in years, but Team Fortress 2 MATTERED to thousands of people. It brought everyone together and formed many friendships, and supplemented the creativity of some of the brightest animators on the internet. It was able to do all of this on such a large scale because it was such a well designed and fully operational game which Valve used to vigilantly upkeep for the lot of a decade.

Some of you might have become aware of the #StopKillingGames movement following the shutdown of The Crew, which involved shutting down the servers and rendering the game completely unplayable with no recourse. It's effectively robbery, but as we see here, there happens to be more than one way to kill a game. A new generation's perception of Team Fortress 2 is forever tainted because of Valve's complete refusal to tackle the bot crisis head on, and these players will never get to experience the joys we had to the fullest.

I can no longer look at this company in a positive light. I guess I should've seen it coming; Valve is not really a game company anymore. Its primary focus is more so digital logistics than anything else, transporting other developers' games to people's computers. It does that job well, but that's about all I can say anymore. Your dreams of a Half-Life 3 release are down the drain, and you're gonna have to accept that this is the new reality of the company. It will take a long time to sink in, but the truth will give you new life.

Point being, you should play G-Darius HD.

If the bots somehow leave or get kicked out, there will be a lot of empty slots, but instead of waiting for new players to connect, the match will start with teams severely unbalanced, with "Player connecting..." messages instead of actual players taking up team slots.
And the cycle continues.

Community servers are much more free from the cheater bots and downtime, but there are few of them and even fewer are pure vanilla.
Single player on a local server is possible, just add built-in bots with console commands or use "TF2 Bot Overhaul" mod for even better experience.

This is my favourite game of all time. Even if it's old, the gameplay is still one of the best experiences I ever had in gaming. I played the Overwatchs, Valorants and The Finals of this world and enjoyed them. But nothing hits as many marks as this game. Sadly, casual mode has been flooded with hacking bots for years now, making it close to impossible to play an evening with you and your buddies without encountering a load of them on every server you get matched on. 

This can go the following ways:
- There are a few bots on the server. Which, after coordinating with your team get votekicked out. Everyone is happy, team 
   numbers are now unbalanced until autobalance decides to do something about it. You can play the game for up to half an 
   hour untill the next bots join the server, repeating the cycle.
- The server you're joining, or the one you cleansed half an hour ago, gets filled with bots that due to their amount or lack 
  of teamcoordination cant be votekicked. Leading to either the bots kicking you from the server, forcing a requeue or you 
  giving up on the server and requeuing yourself willingly.
- The server you get into is a happy place without any bots on which you can play until we cycle back to the first and 
  second point mentioned.

Over the years I had a lot of fun here, played casual, played competitive, participated in the trading community, joined silly community servers, found some of my now closest friends, even a relationship at some point. I have a thousand good memories that I would not want to miss. Now I can't recommend anyone I know to play the game with me. I used to bring people to play with me from other areas of my life and they had a blast. I can't do that nowadays because of the frustrating cycle mentioned above. The game's gameplay and the people in it used to speak for themselves in showing its appeal.

If you read a bit into the bot problem, you start to realize the almost mafia-like structures that seemed to have been built around it and the levels of harassment anyone speaking out against these issues has to face. From doxxing to swatting, everything is possible. You just start to wonder how the hell this could have happened in any way, shape or form.

My biggest hope would be that Valve gets to fix all of this and that I, some months down the line, can add an edit note to this review that says :"Everything is fine again, lol", but I can't do that for now. The last time I heard a Valve employee mention the bot crisis casually, they talked about not doing anything about it.

I haven't bought anything from either the in-game store or the community market related to TF2 items in a while, maybe that could help ... I dont know to be honest. Here is me hoping Valve cares about a revenue stream getting smaller. Even if it's grasping at straws. If I managed to convince one person to join me in that protest, this review was worth it.

Overall, I'm just sad. I used to love this game. If I think about TF2 nowadays, I think back to all the great times I had with it ... and then mentally add: “A shame what happened to it.”

What's left for me from this game? It's either something like TF2Classic, which isn't too hard to set up but not as convenient as clicking install on Steam, leaving a few friends out already. Or joining community servers with playerbases that have a different kind of mindset than the casual experience I'm so fond of.

As a closing statement, I'm going to quote FUNKe from a video he made around 2–3 years ago: 
“I love TF2, and I miss it.”

Reviews are for new players deciding if they want to choose an exciting new game to spend their time on. What then is the new player experience for TF2 in the year 2024? 

You, Bright Eyed New Player, hits the Casual browser and queues into a random Valve-run server. The first experience you are likely to get as soon as you load into a game, even prior to seeing the class select screen? Some bot spamming obnoxious profanities into your ears at max volume. You are then immediately kicked before understanding what is happening.

 A slightly more generous take on what could be your experience, prospective New Player. You choose a class (Lets be real, probably Scout), walk out of spawn, and are immediately headshot by the legion of spinning hackers on the enemy team. You search for the keybind to ask you team what happened only to be greeted by this message "voice/text chat is not allowed on this account". A quick search online tells you that you cannot communicate in any way unless you pay Valve money. Ostensibly this is to counter bots, though you will likely have already encountered many bots spamming racism and hate into the chat and into your ears. You are then promptly kicked from the server. 

So you finally get a server where you aren't immediately kicked in under 10 seconds by spinning bots shouting profanities and actually get to play a round of TF2. Except you are still headshot immediately by a sniper within half a second of leaving spawn. But this cannot be a bot, no, they have hats and are proclaiming in chat that they are human. They even have a couple friends backing them up, so they must certainly just be incredible at the game and using some item to see you through walls and while invisible. You then proceed to have "The most fun you can have online" and are stuck in spawn by a hacker for the whole round with nary a chance of pushing out. 

By all means, if this seems fun for you download the game.
Roll the dice to see which of the above options will be your experience.
Maybe you get astoundingly lucky and get a server that can deal with bots after a few minutes and can play a somewhat normal round.
Its unlikely, but possible.
Maybe you search online and find a server that Valve does not run that is free from bots, queue for a year waiting for a spot to join and immediately get stomped by people with literal thousands of hours of experience. 
This is considered the "Good" option by many players.

This used to be "The Most Fun You Can Have Online" some years ago, but now the game is something you must struggle against to have fun. Truly, I have no idea how a new player is supposed to experience TF2 as it was in the glory days.

this is a really odd review to write. tf2 is one of my favorite games of all time. i adore the gameplay, the characters, the world, fuck, even the hats add a fun extra layer for those who wish to dip their toes into it. i LOVE tf2. and yet, i cannot in good conscience tell anyone new "hey, you should play this game." because they shouldn't.

text:
Christmas Day 2010. After a day of opening presents, late into the night, I open up my laptop next to my older brother and he pulls up this very page, and inputs his credit card details to pay the $20 to buy me this game. This was all I wanted when I was 12. I thought about this game so much it consumed me, and that one generous purchase gave me 13 and a half years of pure joy. I have played or thought about this game for a majority of my lifetime. It is still in my Top 5 favorite of all time.

And it's not just me. This game is a cultural touchstone. Every single one of these characters has been recognized or at least noticed not only by people who have never played TF2, but by people who don't play video games. Their feature in SFM shorts has influenced film making. Its class-based team shooter formula has been copied by titles far more successful than it is today- titles that Valve is now borrowing game elements from. Its characters are a textbook example in visual design. And all of that still isn't enough for Valve to consider giving the game some tender love and care.

And what puzzles me most about this lack of investment is that it seems to be unjustifiable in terms of a business perspective. With this loyal of a fanbase spending regular amounts of money on in-game purchases, and this much of an outcry over the state of a beloved cultural icon, I would only assume that a legitimate update on this game, that would not only fix the bots but also add new content, would get its investment back within minutes of its release, and generate tons of revenue. And we aren't even asking for an update. We're just asking for a fix to the bots, so that we can go back to the game that has defined so many of our lives.

I hope Deadlock succeeds. I genuinely do. Because if it fails, I can only think of one reason why it would- neglect. Valve as a company seems to be infallible in the eyes of its fans. That Photoshop of Gabe Newell as Jesus is so ubiquitous I have no idea what the original looks like. But if Deadlock is going to function as a game, it's going to need a different anti-cheat than VAC. And if Deadlock can use something other than VAC, so can TF2, I can only assume. Maybe that's not the solution. Maybe it's much more complex than that, but Deadlock will face the same challenges TF2 does, and I genuinely believe that fixing TF2 would not come at the cost of their current project. If it would, I would really love to know why. 

This review is rambly now, and I hate editing, so I'll end here. To call TF2 a great game doesn't even make sense. This is one of the most influential pieces of media in the past two decades. And I'm about to uninstall it.

I owe it to this game for the many friends I've found and stayed in touch with for years and over a decade now, but I cannot in good conscience recommend this game in its current state. 

Public server matchmaking, one of the "latest" major features added to it, has been infested with bot accounts that ruin this experience for any casual player, whether through blatant aimbot hacks, chat spam, mic spam, by ejecting you out of a match with votekicks, or by everything of what was mentioned above.

Valve have been neglecting the severity of this issue for years, despite still frequently adding cosmetic items to their in-game store, thus profiting from the game as a product. And even though community servers are still there, available in the server browser like they have been long before matchmaking was implemented, I do not want to spend my time looking for such server, just to have a quick 30-minute quick match to entertain myself. Not to mention any of the potential issues that could come from community servers in forms of gigabytes of content being required to download at awfully low speed, dealing with community elitism or moderators with superiority complex, or abundance of confusing plugins filling the screen. But this isn't about community servers right now, I just wanted to quickly get into a game, and start playing, just like the game offers me to do in their own main menu.

Team Fortress 2 was what could have been considered a classic for its genre, and the matchmaking, while not perfect in practice (team imbalances etc), was still enough to scratch the itch for a quick fun game with people of varying skill degrees and backgrounds. Sure, Valve doesn't owe me or anybody else their time to deal with this problem (although highly debatable, since people are still buying and trading items on the regular, including the marketplace), there is a massive playerbase who's been begging, pleading for them to [u][b]permanently[/b][/u] deal with the ongoing bot crisis in their beloved game.

[i]"TF2 community, we hear you! We love this game and know you do, too. We see how large this issue has become and are working to improve things."[/i]

[url=https://x.com/TeamFortress/status/1529970640224018433]Valve said this in their official TF2 Twitter statement on May 27, 2022.[/url] It has been two years since then, and whatever they've done has only temporarily stifled bot activity, for a very short time. 

Dedicated fans will know that Valve are not a company of many words, but if those are going to be their last words towards the public plea to take action against what could be considered a rampantly increasing artificial plague within their own product, then I have no other option but to leave a negative recommendation and move on.

ORIGINAL REVIEW TEXT:

  TF2 is a classic FPS that endures only due to its passionate fanbase. The characters are still iconic, the gameplay at its best is still fun with a ton of mechanical variety. You can have hour-long games with tense back and forths finally ending in a climactic finish, and you can have silly experiences just hanging around with friends or strangers. You can still have a fun time if you are a longtime veteran of the game, but I cannot recommend it to new players due to the neglect from the developers of the game, Valve. The game is flooded with cheaters, both human and robot. A new player to the game not only needs to learn the actual game mechanics, but also about bots. Things like, "what does a bot name look like?" and "when should you re-queue because a server is unrecoverable and completely lost to bots?" If a new player didn't spend money on the game (a free to play or "F2P"),  they cannot even ASK these questions, because in the last few years Valve disabled chat usage for F2P players.

  The F2P chat ban has not solved the issue of the bots spamming the chat because bot hosters just buy premium for the bots. It's not that expensive for them since it takes months for the bots to be banned, if they even get banned. Instead, it has ruined the experience for new players. New players can't ask about their weapons. They can't chat along with everyone else. They can't even use the hotkey bound by default by the game to call for a medic. Given that the game is a [b]team[/b] game the chat ban has a direct negative effect on the gameplay for the F2P player and their team. Valve could theoretically revert the F2P chat ban at any time just as quickly as they started it. Valve should know by now the chat ban has done nothing to stop bots from spamming the chat, but it remains in place. Is Valve that desperate for bot hoster's money?

  Even with all of these issues, Valve cannot even be bothered to state anything about the game beyond the fact that basically no one is working on the game, nor interested in working on it. Valve claims to want to avoid "treadmill work" where recurring maintenance is needed, but is perfectly fine with the "treadmill work" of releasing new content for people to pay for. More microtransaction crates are added to the game while the game on official Valve servers remains pretty much unplayable if you don't know how to properly navigate those servers in the modern era of TF2. While TF2 may not make anywhere near as much money as Counterstrike, I would assume that it makes enough money to hire a contractor to manually ban obvious cheating spinbots if nothing else.

  While the game isn't dead due to the community who has stuck with it for over a decade, the game [i]will[/i] slowly wither away unless Valve takes action against bots and cheaters, and allows the F2P players to have a voice again. All of which seems very unlikely.

  For anyone who does want to try start playing as a new player regardless, I recommend either avoiding casual or actively taking the time to learn about the bot issue first:
- Look for snipers with robotic non-human movement, huge aim snaps, or aiming straight up 100% of the time to identify bots. Some bots do not play sniper but may still aim straight up or have huge aim snaps.
- Leave servers when one team is 50% full of bots or more.
- Avoid healing bots. Don't push forward when bots are present to be courteous to the enemy team.
- Always kick bots as soon as possible because bots will begin votekicks on real players when they can.
- When a votekick starts, do not vote to kick unless you are sure that the team overwhelmingly believes the player in question to be a bot, or even better, verify the player is actually a bot yourself.
- Keep an eye on the chat to see if anyone is calling out bots on either team. People aren't always correct or truthful, but it does mean you should check on the player in question.
- Avoid certain maps/gamemodes during bot waves (the CTF gamemode and the map Harvest get especially bad).

  As for community servers, "Uncletopia" servers exist but they are not the same as the "true" casual experience that Valve intended. There are class limits and the players tend to be more skilled and more focused on playing the game to win, which is not a bad thing but may not interest all players."Skial" servers are closer to the "vanilla TF2" experience but most of their servers are 24/7 servers for specific maps with only a couple true casual servers. Other "vanilla TF2" casual servers exist but are often empty.

  Although this review may be posted at the same time as many other negative reviews, this review is sincere. I cannot recommend the game to new players anymore.

For whatever it's worth, Valve, fix TF2.

I first downloaded this game in 2013 and, despite dropping off a couple times over the years, it has been a reliably fun game for that entire time. That was until 2020, when a group of degenerate trolls became capable of hosting large numbers of bots that do something very simple: They join Valve servers, pick sniper, and aimbot everything that isn't them. This practice allows these people to shut down dozens of servers simultaneously without even being present at their computers. As a result, it has become largely impossible to play the game without entering community servers, which aren't a proper replacement due to the work required to find a decent community server that can facilitate casual play.

This game has been my go to for many years precisely because new games don't do what this game does. Modern shooters are all focused on one thing: competitive play. The problem is that forced competitive play is bound to turn into a toxic shit flinging fest where everyone hates everyone else including themselves because trying to get 5 other random people to work together is near impossible. The developers of Team Fortress 2 figured this out before even making this game and it's one of the large reasons it has stood the test of time. Even with all the bots and lack of support from Valve this game is simply irreplaceable to me. Other games keep trying and failing to do what TF2 does and it's so frustrating to see this wonderful game fall victim to an awful combination of developer apathy and degenerate jerks trying to ruin it and stop anyone that wants to simply play the game as Valve intended.

I am saying this now because enough is enough. I'm going to continue playing this game but I will not be giving another cent to Valve through this game until they have done what needs to be done to fix these problems and introduce a more permanent solution to the problem. Sure that may sound counter intuitive to keep playing this game but it's not playing the game that keeps the servers alive, at least not just playing. Servers cost money, and without the stream of income from players like me those servers cannot survive. I also won't recommend anyone new play this game for the same reason.

There's also another reason Valve needs to get on this problem: It's not just TF2 anymore, because Counter Strike 2 runs on the source engine (granted it's source 2 rather than source 1), this means that Counter Strike 2 is vulnerable to the same botting problem that TF2 has been subject to for years now. If Valve doesn't take action to fix this, it WILL spill out into their biggest game, and then they'll be forced to act in a way that TF2's community simply can't force.

The ball is in your court Valve, either fix this, or it's going to get worse, it will bring in Counter Strike 2's community, which carries far more weight, and that will be a problem they can't ignore.

EDIT: So it seems they hired a contractor to actually fix the problem. Well I guess I can go back to recommending this game. Better late than never, but time will tell if the bots truly stay away.

2,138-ish hours was my time in Team Fortress 2 in 2019. Since then, it has gone up around 60 hours, and the stunted time is all down to the Bot issues and my repeated attempts to play it. The Bot problems of TF2 are a perfect encapsulation of why VAC doesn't work; it relies too little on automation, too much on manual waves, and there's no work being done in the background to satiate any player who just wants to play Casual.

"But just play community servers". That's [b]NOT[/b] a solution to the problem, that is running away from the issue at hand and circumventing it. Praying to [b][Insert Local Deity of your Religion Here][/b] would be just as effective a solution than just playing on community servers.

Here is the bitter Pill people don't want to swallow, the scroll of truth they continually throw away because what the sought after was too real for them: Valve likes Illegal Gambling. It likes loot boxes, it likes its storefront filled with shoddy asset-flipped games they can't be bothered to sift through or have any semblance of QA for. That is the reality, and people need to start accepting that.

Since 2015, Valve made it big with Lootboxes and weapon skins in CSGO, and since then, has had one thing on their mind, and that has been "How can we players part with their money while still looking like the good guys of PC Gaming?". Turns out, when you have rabid fans who will go for bat to defend you whenever you screw up, you can get away with a lot of stuff. Quelle Surprise that breeds complacency among users and a situation where you can't escape Steam.

The bots of TF2 are emblematic of Valve's Sloth-like tendencies. Unwilling to make any move to solve or fix a problem until they think it's perfection incarnate, lest they be seen as the bad guy or the solution is seen as unfit. text:
Team Fortress 2 represents many firsts for me. It was my first 3D first-person shooter, it was my first non-Flash game, it was my first PvP game, and it was my first Steam game. I remember bragging about getting the Gibus to my friends at school, and even became indebted to a classmate so I could get a Steam card in order to buy hats. I don't think I ever finished paying that debt off.

I don't play this game much anymore - my tastes in gaming have moved on from PvP first-person shooters. However, the culture surrounding Team Fortress 2 is much more than just the people playing the game. The memes, the animations both serious and silly, the YouTube community, the voice actors, and every single kid that put ragdolls into crude poses in Garry's Mod because they were bored. This is what keeps me around.

Game companies everywhere would give their figurative left nuts to have a property that continues to remain pervasive in not just gaming culture, but Internet culture as a whole, even a decade and a half after it's released. And what does Valve do with this unique blessing?

Nothing. Or, at least, close to nothing.

Surely you've heard about the state the game is in. No major updates in years. Cheating bot accounts ruining games. Promises made, but not kept.

It's not like Valve doesn't care at all. They have indeed made some mid-sized updates ever since the original #SaveTF2 campaign, and have even modified the game to take advantage of modern 64-bit hardware. But there still seems to be a collective unwillingness at Valve to sit down, put their heads together, and finally tackle the fundamental problems that have been plaguing the game for close to 33% of its illustrious lifespan.

I know about Valve’s unique organizational structure that discourages people from working on old, unpopular projects. I know about the messy, disorganized state the game is in under the hood. I know about the constant arms race that cheat creators and cheat detectors are in, a race in which silence is often justified.

But it’s still not an excuse to do so little in such a large span of time.

We don’t even want major updates anymore. Those can wait. We just want something, anything, to remove the near-constant threat of bots that ruin games for novice and veteran players alike. Something that isn’t a band-aid solution, like the silencing of F2P accounts was. Something actually concrete. And if you have been working on something, then tell us. Break the silence.

It’s not a matter of resources – Valve has some of the most talented people in the whole industry, and a near–unlimited source of income from Steam. Even if no one at Valve wants to touch the game, or VAC, with a ten foot pole, surely somebody can be paid to do so.

It’s not even just TF2 anymore – recently even Counter-Strike 2 has been seeing an influx of cheating bots that has caused an outcry from their community and their content creators. It is in Valve’s best interest to fix the issues that affect two of their most popular IPs.

At this point, doing nothing would be Valve shooting themselves in the foot. Sure, they could just sit back and let the cash roll in while leaving one, or even two, of their most popular games to the wolves. They could do that. But what would it cost them? Their reputation of one of the greatest game developers of all time. A game that continues to maintain a stable, if smaller than previously thought, player base despite all the problems that plague it. And finally, a dedicated community that wants nothing more than to see their favorite game rise from the ashes of neglect and abuse.

Valve, do something.

#FixTF2

26/08/24 Edit: Things have indeed changed for the better, but this review is remaining negative until it's clear that more permanent measures are going to be put into place. Still, good on you, Valve.

19/09/24 Edit: With recent good news, I feel confident in switching my review to Positive. Give the game a go if you somehow stumble upon this review. There's no better time than now.

We've been 5 years from the last major content update that wasn't community created in-game cosmetics (which Valve profits heavily from) and poorly tested community created maps, or some bug fixes every blue moon.

The code for the majority of these bots is publicly available, which is why community anti-cheat programs work on their servers, getting rid of them is perfectly doable, it's only through lack of care and effort that they exist on Valve servers still, after many years.

text:
I took prolonged breaks from TF2 multiple times but I always find myself coming right back. There is nothing like this game, the humour, the atmosphere, the community. It is an immortal masterpiece. Despite all of its flaws it's still The experience to gain. The sheer fun you can get from playing TF2 is incredible, the age of the game combined with player count speak for themselves. 

Sure there are dated balance issues and some questionable game design choices, but it honestly only adds to the experience. There are very few outright infuriating and unfair matchups one can fing themself in while playing. The answer is always there and  experience in the game always holds the key to winning (minus RNG, of course). There are 9 classes with dozens of playstyles spread across them, there should be something for everyone. For Gods sake, if you despise PvP you can go full pootis throwing sandviches to friend and foe alike or just chill out in friendly community servers, some of which reach VRchat levels of weird interactions.

I decided to write this "review" after recent reality check by Zesty Jesus. Valve, for the love of us all, do something about the bot crisis. It's not about the economy (which is screwed by thousands of tradebots), it's not about the player count (which has actually plummeted back in 2020), it's about reputation. People love this game and many veterans would come back despite the (honestly horrible) MYM matchmaking, refined inflation and other stuff. 
Just a nice big ol' update and a ban wave against bots and it could really start shining again, break the charts and take its place under the sun. I want more people to play this game, to learn what I have started learning more than 10 years ago. Come on, you can even make a new Hired Badge with a supposed update to really distinguish those who stayed with the game in its second Darkest Hour. 

Let's stay strong and hope for the best, like we always have.

If you want to try this game - do it. If you like it - invest in some keys from in-game store and buy a couple of cosmetics. A key is $2.49 and three of them are basically the price of full experience. Yeah, with recent free-to-play voice chat limitations five (yes) bucks have semi-officially become the price tag of the game. Or pick up an Orange Box bundle for all Valve classics included. 
There is a ridiculous amount of really cheap infamous hats, those three keys should be enough to outfit all of your favourite mercs with something stylish. And Style is the second name of TF2.

#SaveTF2 take 2

I started this game accidentally and decided to go through the developer commentary for old time's sake. I listened to the old valve's choices for a bit and studied the models for the game for a bit to see some good designs for 3D models. After thinking a bit, it's saddens me to see how far this game has fallen. 

I grew up with this game. It was one of many what made me choose PC for gaming as I wasn't limited by BS things like online subscriptions and forced controller use. I played so far back that I even got the Cheater's lament. I miss that hat as I was using my dad's account. Racked up a lot of hours and memories. 

Now, I see that TF2 is plagued with bots, both idle and cheater bots that valve refuses to do something about. Items are balanced for competitive, even though the game was never designed to be competitive but a fun silly shooter that has an achievement where you cause a person to rage quit. And doesn't help that the community is far too passive to say no to terrible ideas and seems to be nothing but redditors at times. Though that seems to be the internet as a whole at times.

The more I see this game's current state, as well as a lot of games and media as a whole, the more I want to make something better to replace this garbage we are all getting. We all work hard for our cash, and we should get the best. Even if it is free. 

Valve, what happened? You guys used to be a beacon of good game creators that anyone could use to understand what works. But now, you are no different to the other developers and publishers that hate their own user base and only put out the bare minimum at best. Sad. I can not wait for the day when people form new teams to replace the old companies and say no to the terrible practices and ideas like DEI and loot boxes.

Oh, and to add on to this review, a message to everyone else. Don't rely on "fixtf2." It's ran by ecelebs and redditors that never liked TF2. Take a look at Uncle Dane's servers and the class limits on it. The only ones who can fix TF2 is Valve themselves. It's not up to us to deal the bot hosters. Valve is currently being lazy bums and trend chasers and not utilizing the fact that the bot hosters have committed actual crimes that they could easily get government help no problem. 

Instead of "fixTF2," I like Gabber's suggestion of "Bringbackquickplay." These bots only arrived when matchmaking was introduced, as it automated joining of games. In the meantime, I recommend playing vanilla community servers and do not spend any cash on this game.

This is the cycle of every Team Fortress 2 player ever:

> Download the game.
> Enter your first match.
> Realize you don't know what you're doing.
> Die repeatedly.
> Just before you rage, you find the Ghastly Gibus hat.
> Since all the pro players have cool-looking hats, you are inspired.
> Die repeatedly in different game modes.
> Discover that you are getting a lot of kills as Pyro.
> Be mentally violated by other players calling you a "f2p gibus pyro".
> Get slightly better at the game.
> Die repeatedly.
> Leave the game.

*6 months later.*

> Start to discover TF2 videos on YouTube.
> Realize that there are more classes than just Pyro and Sniper.
> End up wanting to be a pro non-Pyro like all the cool YouTubers.
> Return to Team Fortress 2.
> Die repeatedly.
> Claim that you 'main' Pyro.
> Walk at people and light them on fire mindlessly for a few weeks. Or months.
> Start getting a good K/D ratio on a different class. (If it's Soldier, you can go die.)
> Succumb to peer-pressure and buy hats.
> Discover the Steam community market and buy more hats for less.
> Feel your skill strangely growing as you get more hats.
> More kills. Less deaths.
> You begin to discover the passive players of TF2. (Sandvich hoovies, spycrabs, box shpees, etc.)
> Develop a kindness and sense of friendship towards your fellow TF2 players.
> Start to top-score more often.
> You begin to care about the state of the game.
> Realize that Pyros are overpowered and pointless.
> Start to hate Pyros.
> Start to hate everyone.
> Start to hate the TF2 community.
> You hate everything and everyone, to the point where you start to kill passive players again.
> Ask yourself, "If I hate this game, why do I have ten unusuals and fifteen Australiums? What am I doing?"
> Look at your playtime and begin to hate yourself.
> You dislike yourself more than the game now.
> Contemplate suicide.
> Contemplate religion.
> Question the game.
> Binge-watch STAR_'s 2012-2013 TF2 videos to remind you of a simpler time.
> Sit down and think.
> Realize what you have become.
> Go into a mid-TF2 crisis.
> Except it's not mid-TF2 anymore. You have 1000 hours in-game.
> What is going on?
> WHAT IS TEAM FORTRESS 2?
> WHY DOES THE LIGHT LIE TO ME?
> Quit TF2 forever.
> Come back to it in a week and die to a gibus sniper who taunts after kill.
> Kill yourself.
